bottleneck: Ultra-high-temperature ceramics (UHTCs) such as ZrB2, HfB2, ZrC, and HfC melt above 3000°C, yet oxidize rapidly beyond roughly 1600°C: active oxidation forms gaseous SiO instead of a protective SiO2 scale, and porous, cracked oxide layers spall away under thermal shock. For hypersonic leading edges, combustors, and nose tips enduring 2000–3000°C, no monolithic ceramic survives extended flight; oxygen ingress and thermal-gradient fracture defeat even the best compositions within minutes.
current_state: ZrB2-SiC and HfB2-SiC remain the best available, with superior oxidation resistance to about 1650°C; high-entropy UHTCs with self-healing oxide scales show improved ablation resistance in labs, and carbide coatings developed with Manchester University claim 12x better ablation performance than ZrC. No composition has yet demonstrated reliable reusable service above 2000°C.

title: Ultra-high-temperature ceramic oxidation resistance above 2000°C
why_it_blocks: Reusable hypersonic flight, maneuvering re-entry vehicles, and sustained Mach 5+ cruise all demand leading-edge materials that survive thousands of seconds of extreme heating. Without them, hypersonics remain expendable and single-use, capping progress across defense, space access, and future high-speed transport.
